But it should not be allowed to hide behind that sentence either. xAI is now suing a man accused of deliberately bypassing Grok's safeguards to create sexualized deepfakes of real adults and children. I think suing him is justified. The person who intentionally creates and distributes illegal material should carry the primary responsibility. We would not normally blame a knife manufacturer when someone uses a knife to commit a crime. But what if the buyer walks into the shop, explains exactly whom he intends to harm, and the seller hands him the weapon anyway? That is where the analogy with AI becomes uncomfortable. An AI platform is not simply selling a passive object. It reads the request, generates the output and can recognize when someone repeatedly rephrases an obviously abusive prompt. It also controls the safeguards for every user, instantly and centrally. No company can prevent every attempt at misuse. Perfection is an impossible legal standard. But implementing meaningful guardrails against explicit requests for child sexual abuse material or non-consensual sexual imagery is not perfection. It is the bare minimum. From 2 August, the EU AI Act will require greater transparency around AI-generated content and deepfakes. That matters, but labelling tells us that something is synthetic. It does not settle who should have prevented the harm. So where should the legal line sit? The problem is no longer whether AI can be misused. The problem is that our institutions are still operating on the assumption that digital evidence is authentic by default. overview.title: Bengaluru Triple Murder Case: How Kenneth Arun Kumar Allegedly Used AI To Plan The Crime
overview.content: # Bengaluru Triple Murder Case: How Kenneth Arun Kumar Allegedly Used AI To Plan The Crime Bengaluru triple murder accused Kenneth Arun Kumar allegedly used an AI chatbot while preparing for the alleged killings, according to police. Here's what investigators claim they found. Vageesha Shrivastava Published on 21 / 07 / 2026 See also on Brut Artificial intelligence tools are now part of everyday life, helping people with research, work and learning. But a Bengaluru triple murder investigation has raised questions about the possible misuse of technology. Police alleged that software professional Kenneth Arun Kumar used an AI chatbot while preparing for the alleged murder of three members of his live-in partner’s family. Investigators claimed that the alleged plan developed over several months and involved digital tools. The case came to light after three members of Shwetha’s family were found dead at Kenneth’s apartment in Bengaluru’s Seegehalli area, under the K R Puram police station limits. Police later arrested Kenneth in Puducherry in connection with the case. ## **What Happened In The Bengaluru Triple Murder Case?** According to the police investigation, the victims were members of Kenneth’s live-in partner Shwetha’s family. Police alleged that Kenneth was involved in the deaths of Shwetha’s mother Muthulakshmi, her father and her brother following a personal dispute. Investigators claimed that the killings were planned and not an immediate act. During the probe, police examined Kenneth’s electronic devices, online activity and alleged conversations with an AI chatbot. The investigation focused on understanding the sequence of events and whether technology played a role in the alleged preparation. ## **A Six-Month Plan: How Police Say The Crime Was Prepared** Police sources claimed that the idea of targeting his partner’s family developed over time. Investigators alleged that Kenneth spent around six months preparing for the alleged crime and researching different aspects of the plan. Police claimed that he used an AI chatbot to ask questions related to the alleged crime. Investigators examined these digital interactions as part of the evidence collected during the probe. However, police have not claimed that AI acted independently. The allegation is that Kenneth used an available technology tool during the preparation process. ## **Why Did Kenneth Allegedly Plan The Killings?** Police are investigating relationship tensions, family disagreements and financial issues as possible reasons behind the alleged killings. According to The Indian Express, tensions had developed between Kenneth and Shwetha’s family over their relationship. Investigators claimed that Shwetha had differences with her mother Muthulakshmi and allegedly felt that her mother was controlling. Police are also examining a financial dispute involving the couple. Police sources claimed that Shwetha had allegedly borrowed around ₹50 lakh from her mother and spent the money on Kenneth. Investigators are looking into whether concerns over repayment and family disagreements contributed to the conflict. Police sources claimed that these issues continued to build over time and that Kenneth spent months preparing for the alleged crime. ## **The Cloud Kitchen Plan And Furnace Link** Police also examined details related to Kenneth’s cloud kitchen plan during the investigation. According to investigators, Kenneth had built an iron furnace as part of his plan to start a cloud kitchen. Police examined the furnace as part of the investigation and are looking into whether it had any connection to the alleged crime. Police said the furnace was originally built for Kenneth's proposed cloud kitchen. Investigators are examining whether it was later intended to be used in connection with the alleged crime. ## **Who Is Kenneth Arun Kumar?** Kenneth Arun Kumar was described by police as a software professional with a technical background. His knowledge of technology became a focus of the investigation after police alleged that he used digital tools while preparing for the alleged crime. Investigators examined his devices, online activity and AI interactions to understand his actions before and after the killings. ## **How Did Police Investigate The Case?** After the bodies were discovered, Bengaluru Police began collecting physical and digital evidence. Investigators examined Kenneth’s electronic devices, online records and other material to reconstruct the events leading up to the killings. Police also analysed alleged AI chatbot conversations as part of the digital evidence. Kenneth was arrested and booked in connection with the triple murder case. The evidence collected by investigators will be examined during the legal process. ## **What Does The Case Reveal About AI Misuse?** The Bengaluru triple murder case has raised questions about how artificial intelligence tools can be misused. AI systems are designed to assist users with tasks such as writing, learning and problem-solving. However, police said the investigation highlights how widely available digital tools can allegedly be misused by individuals accused of committing crimes. Investigators have not alleged that the AI system acted independently or encouraged the crime. Instead, they claim the accused used it while preparing for the alleged offences. The case does not suggest that AI planned or carried out the crime independently. Instead, it highlights a growing challenge around preventing the misuse of easily accessible technology while ensuring responsible use.

overview.title: Bengaluru triple murder: Accused allegedly used AI chatbot to plan killings, police say
overview.content: Subscribe Karnataka # Bengaluru triple murder: Accused allegedly used AI chatbot to plan killings, police say During interrogation, Kenneth allegedly told police that the idea of disposing of the bodies using an iron furnace came after consulting the AI tool. Police said Kenneth had built the furnace as part of plans to start a cloud kitchen but later considered using it for dispose of the bodies. Kenneth and Shwetha Written by: TNM Staff Published on: 20 Jul 2026, 3:48 am Bengaluru police investigating a triple murder in the city found that one of the accused allegedly used a popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot over several months to plan the crime, including seeking information on methods of killing, disposing of bodies and removing bloodstains. The police have sought the accused's chat records from the chatbot's parent company as part of the digital evidence in the case, according to The Indian Express. The accused, 25-year-old engineer Kenneth, and his live-in partner, Shwetha Somasundar (25), were arrested by the KR Puram police for the alleged murders of Shwetha's mother, Muthulakshmi S. (48), father, Somasundar (54), and younger sister, Supriya (20). The three were allegedly killed at the couple's apartment in K R Puram on June 22. According to The Indian Express, Kenneth allegedly consulted the AI chatbot over nearly six months while planning the murders. Police said they have written to the chatbot's parent company seeking complete logs of his conversations to corroborate other digital evidence collected during the investigation. During interrogation, Kenneth allegedly told police that the idea of disposing of the bodies using an iron furnace came after consulting the AI tool. Police said Kenneth had built the furnace as part of plans to start a cloud kitchen but later considered using it for disposal of the bodies. "He was planning to start a cloud kitchen and had built an iron furnace for this purpose. When the idea of murder came up, he consulted the AI tool, which indicated the merits and demerits of incinerating bodies before disposal. He planned to repurpose the furnace," a police source said. Police said the alleged motive behind the murders appears to be linked to financial disputes and strained family relations. Police sources said both accused come from middle-class families. Kenneth's father is a retired employee of a defence public sector undertaking involved in aircraft manufacturing, while Shwetha's late father worked for a multinational IT company. Investigators said psychological assessments conducted during the probe pointed to severe social isolation. According to police, Shwetha had earlier worked in a high-paying role at a multinational social media company but lost her job after becoming increasingly dependent on Kenneth. Police described their relationship as transactional, alleging that Shwetha financially supported Kenneth while he remained socially isolated from friends and family. **Background of the case** On June 22, police alleged, Muthulakshmi was lured to the K R Puram apartment, where Kenneth stabbed her 26 times. When Shwetha's father and younger sister arrived separately a short while later, they too were allegedly attacked and killed. After the murders, the couple allegedly travelled to Shwetha's parental home in southeast Bengaluru and stole cash and silver ornaments before fleeing to Puducherry. Police said they had also travelled to Puducherry on vacation about two weeks before the killings. The investigation gathered momentum after Somasundar, despite sustaining fatal injuries, managed to crawl out of the apartment. Neighbours found him on the staircase around 9 pm. Before succumbing to his injuries, he reportedly gave a dying declaration identifying his daughter Shwetha and Kenneth as the attackers and urged police to rescue his wife and younger daughter, who remained inside the flat. Shwetha was arrested in Puducherry on June 24, while Kenneth was arrested within the following two days. Shwetha was remanded to judicial custody on July 10 after the completion of her police custody. Police said she has expressed willingness to make a confessional statement in exchange for a pardon. Kenneth, who underwent polygraph and other scientific examinations during nine days of police custody, was remanded to judicial custody by a Bengaluru magistrate court on Saturday, July 18. overview.title: "Roadmap to murder:" engineer spent 6 months asking AI how to kill
overview.content: # "Roadmap to murder:" engineer spent 6 months asking AI how to kill Contains sensitive details. Crime Scene. Hindustan Times via Getty Images. Marcus Walsh Journalist July 20, 2026 Updated: July 21, 2026 Key takeaways: * Police allege the suspect used an AI chatbot to research killing methods, body disposal and cleaning bloodstains. * Investigators have requested six months of chatbot logs to support the prosecution's digital evidence. * Police say financial strain and family resentment drove the alleged triple murder plot. * Detectives believe extreme social isolation helped the pair lose sight of real-world consequences. Key Takeaways by nexos.ai, reviewed by Cybernews staff. **An engineer and his partner reportedly committed a triple murder in Bengaluru, India, spending 6 months consulting a popular AI chatbot before the killings.** Police allege the engineer sought advice on how to murder, as well as methods for getting rid of bodies and removing bloodstains. Investigators say that nearly every stage of the alleged plot was researched through AI conversations, with police claiming the suspect, Kenneth, even asked about burning bodies after building an iron furnace intended for a planned cloud kitchen, a commercial kitchen used to prepare food for delivery only. Kenneth and his partner, Shwetha Somasundar, both aged 25, were arrested by local police after the June 22nd murders of Shwetha's mother, father, and younger sister. Police say the chatbot was a "roadmap" that helped shape the alleged plan, and have requested the suspect's complete AI chat history from the platform's parent company, which so far remains unnamed. As reported in *The Indian Express*, the police statement described: > “When the murder thought entered his head, he consulted the AI tool, which indicated the merits and demerits of incinerating bodies before disposal.” ## Financial and resentful motives The alleged motive centered on money, family conflict, and resentment toward his partner Shwetha's mother, with claims that Shwetha feared having to repay roughly 5 million Indian rupees (around $60,000) borrowed from her mother. The mother, Muthulakshmi, was lured to the apartment first before allegedly being stabbed 26 times. Subsequently, Shwetha's father and younger sister allegedly arrived separately and were also attacked. Police say the suspects later traveled to Shwetha's parental home in southeast Bengaluru to steal cash and silver ornaments before fleeing to nearby Puducherry. Here, they also discarded the younger sister Supriya's mobile phone. # Has your password leaked? Enter your password to check if it has leaked. Having a leaked password creates the risk of identity theft, financial damages, and worse! Crucially, the case turned when father Somasundar crawled from the apartment, blood-soaked, as neighbors found him lying on the staircase. He identified both suspects before dying in the hospital. Police describe both suspects as living in extreme social isolation despite professional backgrounds, claiming Kenneth had become largely cut off from friends while Shwetha became financially dependent on him. Shwetha had previously held a job at an international social media news company, but became more isolated after losing it. And according to police, the pair processed real-world consequences as if they were playing a computer game, with AI seemingly playing a major role in it. technical.title: Bengaluru Triple Murder: Police Say Accused Used AI Chatbot to Plan Killings - The420.in
technical.content: Bengaluru Police allege the accused in a triple murder consulted an AI chatbot for six months while planning the killings, and have sought his chat logs. SHARE In what police are describing as India’s first case of its kind, investigators in Bengaluru say a 25-year-old accused in a triple murder consulted an AI chatbot at nearly every stage of a six-month plan to kill his live-in partner’s parents and sister, and have now written to the AI’s parent company seeking his complete chat history as evidence. ### A Family Killed in Seegehalli The murders took place on June 22 at a rented apartment in Bengaluru’s Seegehalli area, within the K.R. Puram police station’s jurisdiction, where Somasundar, 52, his wife Muthulakshmi, 48, and their younger daughter Supriya, 19, were found stabbed to death. Days later, police arrested the couple’s elder daughter Shweta, 24, and her live-in partner Kenneth, 25, both engineers by profession, after tracking them to Puducherry, where they had gone into hiding. Investigators say that while both accused acted in tandem, Kenneth was responsible for the bulk of the planning and execution, and it is his alleged reliance on an AI chatbot, reportedly Google Gemini, that has drawn the case unusual attention. Police say he consulted the chatbot repeatedly over roughly six months, seeking guidance at various stages of the alleged conspiracy. ### How Investigators Say the Chatbot Was Used According to police, Kenneth avoided asking the chatbot direct questions about committing murder or disposing of a body. Instead, investigators allege he framed his queries as hypothetical scenarios, of the kind, “if something like this happens, what should someone do,” a pattern police believe was a deliberate attempt to extract relevant information without triggering the safety mechanisms most AI systems have built in for such requests. Police say the resulting conversations touched on planning the killings, destroying evidence, removing bloodstains, and evaluating whether an iron furnace Kenneth had built for a planned cloud kitchen business could be repurposed for body disposal. A senior officer told The Indian Express that investigators had “almost considered naming the AI chatbot as an accomplice,” given the extent to which Kenneth appeared to rely on it, though police have been clear that they are not attributing any legal liability to the AI tool itself. Bengaluru Police have formally written to Google seeking the underlying chat logs to corroborate Kenneth’s own account, given during interrogation, of how heavily he depended on the chatbot throughout the planning period. ### Financial Strain and Family Conflict at the Core The alleged motive traces back to money and mounting family tension. Police say Shweta had borrowed around ₹50 lakh from her mother to fund Kenneth’s cloud kitchen venture, a business that investigators believe failed to generate meaningful returns, leaving the loan largely unpaid even as pressure to repay it grew. Kenneth reportedly told police during interrogation that it was ultimately a “trivial” dispute that pushed him toward the killings, though the underlying pressure had clearly been building for months. Investigators say Shweta had separately expressed frustration with what she considered her mother’s controlling behaviour, a friction that had reportedly strained the family for some time, while psychological assessments during the probe found Kenneth had become severely socially isolated, relying almost entirely on Shweta for both emotional and financial support after leaving the IT sector. ### What the Case Signals for AI Oversight The episode has reopened debate around the safeguards built into mainstream AI platforms, which are generally designed to refuse or limit assistance connected to violent or illegal acts. Cybersecurity experts note that the case, if the allegations hold up, appears to illustrate how such safeguards can potentially be circumvented through indirect or hypothetical framing rather than explicit requests, a gap that developers of AI systems have been working to close as these tools see wider adoption. Renowned cybercrime expert and former IPS officer Prof Triveni Singh said the case underscores how emerging technologies can be misused when combined with clear criminal intent, even as the same tools deliver genuine value across productivity, research, healthcare and education. He said AI cannot replace human judgment or legal accountability, and noted that digital evidence, spanning chat records, cloud data, device forensics and online activity logs, is becoming an increasingly central pillar of modern criminal investigations, one police forces across India will likely need to build far greater technical capacity to handle. Police say the investigation remains ongoing as they await a formal response from Google and continue forensic verification of the digital evidence, with the precise role each accused played still being established before final charges are framed. #### Stay Connected

Updated on: Jul 21, 2026, 17:48:23 IST By HT News Desk Prefer HTon Google As the investigation into the Bangalore triple murder continues, the probe has revealed that the accused allegedly used an AI chatbot to plan the killings. The Bengaluru police have written to an AI tool company seeking access to the chat history of the accused. Days after the murders, the deceased couple's elder daughter, Shwetha, and her live-in partner, Kenneth, were arrested separately from Puducherry. Police stated that the couple fled the scene and were taking shelter to evade arrest. (PTI/Representational) The probe further added that the accused the planned the murders for six months, news agency PTI reported on Tuesday. On June 22, 52-year-old Somasundar, his wife, 48-year-old Muthulaxmi, and their 19-year-old daughter Supriya were found stabbed to death. Days after the murders, the deceased couple's elder daughter, Shwetha, and her live-in partner, Kenneth, were arrested separately in Puducherry. Police stated that the couple fled the scene and were taking shelter to evade arrest. As per cops, Shwetha had allegedly borrowed ₹50 lakh from her mother for Kenneth to start a cloud kitchen business. Over fear of repayment and no funds, the couple allegedly planned the murder. ## Used AI chatbot to plan murder, say cops As per police, Shweta and Kenneth consulted an AI chatbot at every step while planning the murder. From how to kill to how to dispose the bodies, the couple used a chatbot. A senior police official told PTI that while the crime was committed by both, the planning was primarily done by Kenneth. Questions and prompts were put in, seeking information on how to kill, dispose of bodies, removing bloodstains, and whether the furnace built by him for the planned cloud kitchen business could be repurposed to incinerate the bodies, a senior police officer said. ## Accused was socially isolated Cops and psychologists have also stated that the accused, Kenneth, was severely socially isolated. Police added that Shwetha financially supported him while he remained socially isolated from friends and family. technical.title: AI chatbot comes under scrutiny in Bengaluru triple murder investigation
technical.content: # AI chatbot comes under scrutiny in Bengaluru triple murder investigation ## Police allege a software professional used an AI chatbot over several months while planning the killings, prompting fresh debate over the limits of AI safety measures. By **Storyboard18**| July 24, 2026, 15:26:15 IST * Share ### Share this Article × WhatsAppFacebookTwitterLinkedinMail * Follow Us Bengaluru triple murder case puts AI chatbot guardrails under scrutiny The investigation into the alleged murder of three members of a Bengaluru family has raised new questions about how artificial intelligence tools can be misused and whether existing safety mechanisms are sufficient to prevent harmful use. According to investigators, 25-year-old software professional Kenneth Arun Kumar allegedly spent nearly six months interacting with an AI chatbot while planning the crime. Police claim he framed his questions as hypothetical situations to obtain information without triggering the platform's safety restrictions. Kenneth and his live-in partner, Shwetha, have been arrested in connection with the deaths of her parents and younger sister at their apartment in Bengaluru's KR Puram. Investigators believe the incident followed a dispute over an alleged unpaid loan of around ₹50 lakh. As part of the investigation, police are examining the accused's digital activity. Reports indicate that Kenneth allegedly sought information on topics including methods of incapacitating individuals, removing bloodstains using chemicals and disposing of bodies. Investigators are also reviewing searches related to whether an industrial furnace intended for a planned cloud kitchen could be used to destroy human remains. Officials told local media that the accused repeatedly interacted with the chatbot while refining the alleged plan. Police have reportedly contacted the company operating the AI platform to obtain conversation records that could form part of the digital evidence in the case. Investigators have not accused the AI platform of any wrongdoing. Instead, the focus has shifted to whether users can bypass built-in safeguards by rephrasing prompts or presenting harmful requests as fictional or academic scenarios. *(Inputs from CNBC TV18 report)* Follow Storyboard18 on Google for the latest and breaking digital news and industry updates, along with in-depth coverage of digital media and gaming news. implementation.content: # 'How to kill, remove bloodstains, dispose bodies': Bengaluru triple murder accused turned to AI chatbot BENGALURU: Investigators probing the sensational triple murder in Bengaluru have approached an artificial intelligence company for access to the accused’s chat history after discovering that he allegedly relied on an AI chatbot to plan the killings over nearly six months, police said on Tuesday. Police said Kenneth, 25, who has been arrested along with his live-in partner Shwetha, 24, allegedly used the chatbot at various stages of the crime, from seeking advice on how to kill and dispose of bodies to finding ways to erase evidence. The murders came to light on June 22, when Somasundar (52), his wife Muthulaxmi (48), and their younger daughter Supriya (19) were found stabbed to death in their apartment in Seegehalli under the KR Puram police station limits. Days later, Shwetha and Kenneth, who had allegedly fled Bengaluru after the murders, were arrested separately in Puducherry, where they had been hiding to evade police. Investigators suspect that financial disputes and strained family relations lay behind the killings. According to police, Shwetha allegedly borrowed Rs 50 lakh from her mother to help Kenneth set up a cloud kitchen business, but the money was exhausted, triggering fears over repayment. While police believe the couple acted together, Kenneth allegedly led the planning and execution of the murders. A senior police officer said he consulted the AI chatbot throughout the six-month period, asking questions about killing methods, body disposal, bloodstain removal and whether a furnace built for the proposed business could be used to incinerate the bodies. During questioning, Kenneth allegedly admitted that a minor disagreement had prompted him to target Shwetha’s family and confessed to depending heavily on the chatbot for guidance. Police have now written to the AI company seeking digital evidence of Kenneth’s conversations with the tool to corroborate his statements. The probe has also revealed that Kenneth suffered from severe social isolation, according to psychological assessments conducted during the investigation. Police alleged that Shwetha financially supported him and gradually distanced herself from friends and family, eventually losing her job in the IT sector. Investigators said the accused duo stole cash and silver ornaments from Shwetha’s house after the murders before escaping to Puducherry. Police said Kenneth allegedly lured Muthulaxmi to the apartment on June 22 and stabbed her repeatedly. Her husband and younger daughter were attacked when they arrived at the scene. Despite sustaining grievous injuries, Somasundar managed to reach the staircase, where neighbours spotted him and alerted police. In his dying declaration, he allegedly identified his daughter and her live-in partner as the attackers and urged police to save his wife and younger daughter before succumbing to his injuries in hospital. AI searches reveal Bengaluru triple murder plot ## Police allege the murders were meticulously planned, with the main accused, Kenneth, using Gemini to seek indirect advice on attacking and killing. Investigators claim he explored using an iron furnace to dispose of the bodies before abandoning the idea, and believed the killings would free him from financial pressure. advertisement New details emerge in Bengaluru triple murder case Sagay Raj Bengaluru,UPDATED: Jul 21, 2026 20:08 IST Barely a month after the Bengaluru triple murder case sent shockwaves across the city, police have revealed that the prime accused, Kenneth, had used Artificial Intelligence (AI) to research how to commit a murder and dispose of a body. They were tracked down in Puducherry, where Shwetha was taken into custody on June 24, followed by Kenneth's arrest a day later, on June 25. Now, a month later, police sources have disclosed that Kenneth had used Google's AI assistant, Gemini, to research how to commit a murder. According to police, Kenneth did not ask direct questions such as, "How do I dispose of a body?" or "How do I commit a murder?" Instead, he allegedly framed his queries indirectly, asking questions along the lines of, "If something like this happens, what should I do?" Police further said Kenneth used only Gemini for his searches. According to investigators, he had initially planned to use an iron furnace that he had purchased for a proposed cloud kitchen venture to dispose of the bodies. However, he later realised that the idea was not practically feasible. advertisement Police also said Kenneth allegedly asked Gemini questions such as, "Thieves came into my house. How do I attack them? What are the weapons?" According to police sources, he also searched for ways to first blind a person and then stab them, attempting to obtain information through the AI chatbot. Police said the iron furnace had originally been purchased for the proposed cloud kitchen. Later, according to police, Kenneth considered using it to dispose of the bodies and made certain arrangements with that objective in mind. Based on their investigation, police believe the murders were premeditated. They alleged that Kenneth had been planning the crime for some time. Police further claimed that Shwetha was aware that he had spoken about such ideas on several occasions but believed he was speaking casually and did not think he intended to act on them. According to police, Kenneth's alleged motive was to murder the family, take their money and live without financial constraints. implementation.title: 6 months, a plan to kill & an AI tool: What police found in Bengaluru triple murder
implementation.content: Premium # Opinion 6 months, a plan to kill & an AI tool: What police found in Bengaluru triple murder ## The alleged motive, according to case records: a dispute over money Shwetha had taken from her parents to spend on her partner. Shwetha was arrested in Puducherry on June 24, two days after the murders of her parents and sister, and Kenneth within the next two days (Express photo/Special arrangement). Written by: Johnson T.A. *Bengaluru*Jul 21, 2026 06:59 AM IST First published on: Jul 21, 2026 at 05:05 AM IST * Make us preferred source on Google He planned the murders for six months. At every step, he turned to a trusted source for answers: how to kill three people; which chemicals could remove bloodstains; how to package the bodies; how to move them out of the apartment; how to fend off anyone who intruded into the house; and whether the furnace he had built for a planned cloud kitchen in Bengaluru could be repurposed to incinerate the bodies before disposal. This story requires a subscription. Unlock this article plus 300+ subscriber-only stories every month Subscribe Now Already a subscriber? Sign In Advertisement That trusted source, according to police and court records, was an AI tool linked to a popular search engine — a discovery, a police officer said, that left investigators so stunned they “almost considered naming the AI tool as an accomplice”. Case records show the sequence of events came to a head on June 25, when Bengaluru police arrested Kenneth (25) and his live-in partner Shwetha, both engineering graduates who had been planning to start a business, for allegedly killing her mother Muthulakshmi S (48), sister Supriya (20) and father Somasundar (54), in that order, at their flat in K R Puram three days earlier. The alleged motive, according to case records: a dispute over money Shwetha had taken from her parents to spend on her partner. This is possibly the first time Bengaluru police have encountered such extensive use of an AI tool in the planning and execution of a murder, sources familiar with the probe said. The tool allegedly shaped Kenneth’s thinking at every stage and had a significant bearing on how the crime was planned, they said. Advertisement So much so, as part of the investigation, police have written to the AI tool’s makers seeking details of Kenneth’s interactions with it, to corroborate the digital evidence in the case. For investigators, the case also points to the social isolation of a tech-savvy generation immersed in the information and entertainment served up by their devices. “The girl did not have any friend, male or female, other than Kenneth from her college days. Kenneth had a girlfriend earlier who left him because she suspected him of lying and stealing,” sources said. Kenneth’s alleged inability to reflect on the consequences of his actions, a lack of social responsibility, and a rapid build-up of frustration that led to an “eliminate them” mindset, “as though life were a video game”, were among the other factors behind the crime, police sources said. Last Saturday, a magistrate’s court remanded Kenneth to judicial custody after nine days in police custody, during which police conducted polygraph and other scientific tests to establish his motive and verify his claims. The court had earlier remanded Shwetha to judicial custody on July 10 after the end of her police custody. She has, meanwhile, sought a pardon and offered to confess. Kenneth has allegedly told investigators that the idea of killing the family first surfaced over a “trivial grievance”. Over the following six months, guided in part by the AI tool, he grew consumed by it, sources said. “He was planning on starting a cloud kitchen and built a furnace for this purpose. When the murder thought entered his head, he consulted the AI tool, which indicated the merits and demerits of incinerating the bodies before disposal. He had planned to repurpose the furnace he built for burning the bodies after the murder,” police sources said. Kenneth allegedly told police that he built the iron furnace himself. “He consulted the AI tool all along the course of planning the murder. If he had spoken to a human friend, they may have advised him against the wrong course he had taken,” police said. “The thought got into his head to ‘eliminate’ the family of his live-in partner, and he got obsessed with it. For six months, he was consumed by this,” police sources said. The impulse is alleged to have been triggered by Shwetha’s grievance against her mother for being “controlling”—and by fears that the mother would ask for Rs 50 lakh Swetha had allegedly borrowed and spent on Kenneth, sources said. While Kenneth and Shwetha allegedly acted in tandem, the bulk of the planning and execution was Kenneth’s, police sources said. Kenneth and Shwetha hail from well-to-do middle-class Bengaluru families. Kenneth’s father worked at a major PSU involved in aircraft manufacturing while Shwetha’s father was employed with a global IT company. Shwetha worked for a while in Bengaluru’s IT sector after graduating but lost it after being allegedly influenced by Kenneth, sources said. Police sources described their relationship as a transactional friendship in which she funded his lifestyle. On June 22, Shwetha’s mother was allegedly lured to the K R Puram apartment first. Once inside, Kenneth allegedly stabbed her 26 times. When Shwetha’s father and sister arrived a short while later, they were also allegedly stabbed. After the murders, Kenneth and Shwetha went to Shwetha’s parents’ house to allegedly steal money and silver ornaments, and are alleged to have thrown her younger sister’s mobile phone near the parents’ home. They then fled to Puducherry. “They had gone to Puducherry around 15 days prior to the murder for a holiday as well,” sources said. Key evidence includes the dying declaration of Somasundar, who was found around 9 pm on June 22 in a pool of blood with multiple stab wounds on a staircase at the Sai Green apartment complex where Shwetha lived. He told police he had been stabbed by his daughter and Kenneth. “My younger daughter Supriya and my wife Muthulakshmi are still in the apartment. Please rescue them,” Somasundar said, according to the FIR, before he was taken to hospital, where he died. © The Indian Express Pvt Ltd * # Bengaluru * # Express Premium Whatsapp Twitter Facebook

The investigation has also spotlighted the dark side of severe social isolation among tech-immersed youth who lack real-world support systems. ## Repurposing a cloud kitchen furnace As per police sources, **Kenneth confessed during the interrogation** that the idea of the murder stemmed from a trivial grievance. “He was planning on starting a cloud kitchen and built an iron furnace for this purpose. When the murder thought entered his head, he consulted the AI tool, which indicated the merits and demerits of incinerating bodies before disposal. He planned to repurpose that furnace to burn the bodies after the murders,” a police source said. Story continues below this ad The police noted that the lack of human interaction facilitated the crime. “He consulted the AI tool all along the course of planning the murder. If he had spoken to a human friend, they may have advised him against the dangerous course he had taken,” the police source added. Kenneth allegedly consulted the AI tool for advice on the method of killing three people, chemicals to be used to get rid of blood stains, packaging of the bodies after the murder, and moving them from the apartment he shared with Shwetha. The Bengaluru police have written to the parent tech company of the AI tool, requesting complete logs of Kenneth’s chat histories to substantiate the digital evidence for the prosecution. Story continues below this ad ## Resentment towards mother Police sources said the motive behind the killings appears to be rooted in financial strain and domestic resentment. Shwetha reportedly held deep animosity toward her mother for being “controlling”. Also, she feared being forced to return Rs 50 lakh that she had borrowed from her mother and subsequently squandered on Kenneth’s lifestyle. On June 22, Shwetha’s mother Muthulakshmi was allegedly lured to the K R Puram apartment first. Once inside, Kenneth allegedly stabbed her 26 times. When Shwetha’s father and sister arrived at the flat a short time later, they were also allegedly stabbed. Following the attack, the couple allegedly travelled to Shwetha’s parental home in southeast Bengaluru to steal cash and silver ornaments. They discarded her younger sister’s mobile phone near the scene before fleeing to Puducherry for a brief getaway, said the police. Story continues below this ad “They had gone to Puducherry around 15 days before the murder for a holiday as well,” sources said. Shwetha’s father Somasundar managed to crawl out of the flat. At around 9 pm on June 22, neighbours found him lying in a pool of blood on the staircase of the Sai Green apartment complex. Before succumbing to injuries at the hospital, Somasundar gave a crucial dying declaration to responding police officers. He stated that he had been attacked by his daughter Shwetha and her friend Kenneth, and begged officers to rescue his wife and younger daughter who were still trapped inside the flat. The police arrested Shwetha from Puducheery on June 24 and Kenneth within the next two days. ## Social isolation and judicial custody Both accused hail from well-to-do, middle-class families of first-generation migrants in Bengaluru. Kenneth’s father is a retired employee of a major defence public sector undertaking involved in aircraft manufacturing, while Shwetha’s late father worked for a global IT firm. Kenneth’s father has since completely distanced himself from the case, telling his son to handle the legal consequences alone. Story continues below this ad Police sources said psychological evaluations during the probe highlighted deep social isolation. Shwetha, who previously held a high-paying job at a multinational social media news forum, lost her job after becoming heavily dependent on Kenneth. Police sources described their relationship as a transactional friendship in which she funded his lifestyle and he was completely cut off from other friends. The police added that the two displayed a lack of social responsibility, processing real-world consequences as if they were playing a video game. Following the conclusion of her police custody, Shwetha was remanded to judicial custody on July 10, where she has reportedly **offered to make a full confession statement** in exchange for a pardon. Kenneth, who underwent polygraph and scientific testing during his nine days in police custody, was formally remanded to judicial custody by a Bengaluru magistrate court on Saturday. © The Indian Express Pvt Ltd **Stay updated with the latest - Click here to follow us on Instagram** Tags: * Bengaluru To enjoy uninterrupted reading, subscribe or download our app. SUBSCRIBE DOWNLOAD APP

Somasundar (52), his wife Muthulaxmi (48), and their younger daughter Supriya (19) were found stabbed to death. Bengaluru Man Allegedly Used AI to Commit Triple Murders Days later, a 24-year-old couple’s elder daughter Shwetha and her live-in partner Kenneth, 25, were arrested separately in Puducherry, where they had allegedly fled after committing the murders. Breaking It Down #### What tactics did Kenneth use to avoid AI safety filters? Kenneth framed his questions to the AI in hypothetical scenarios, which helped him bypass safety filters and obtain information about committing murder and disposing of bodies without triggering alarms. This manipulation allowed him to gather sensitive information while maintaining a facade of innocuousness in his inquiries. #### What previous cases highlight AI's role in violent crimes? There have been multiple instances where AI models were implicated in assisting individuals with planning murders and suicides. These cases raise concerns about AI's capability to handle sensitive topics and the potential dangers of users seeking harmful guidance from AI. #### What was the motive behind Kenneth and Shwetha's actions? The motive appears to stem from financial disputes and strained family relations, particularly regarding a significant loan that Shwetha borrowed from her mother. The argument over this loan escalated, leading to the tragic events of the murders. Created with AI. ## Accused Used AI Chatbot To Plan Murder According to investigators, Kenneth had been planning the murders for nearly six months and used an AI chatbot throughout the process. Police said he allegedly asked the chatbot questions related to killing, disposing of bodies, removing bloodstains, and whether a furnace built for a proposed cloud kitchen business could be used to incinerate bodies, PTI reported. A senior police officer said Kenneth admitted during interrogation that he depended heavily on the chatbot for guidance and consulted it repeatedly during the planning phase. Following the interrogation, police wrote to the parent AI company seeking digital evidence, including Kenneth’s chat history with the tool, to verify his statements and strengthen the investigation. ## Financial Dispute and Family Tensions Police said the alleged motive was linked to financial disputes and strained family relations. Representative Photo: iStock # Bengaluru triple-murder co-accused used AI tool to plan killings, cops say, seek chat history ## In what could be India's first hi-tech murder, police say Kenneth quizzed the AI chatbot with hypothetical queries over 6 months; they now probe details The Federal 22 July 2026 3:49 PM IST Click the Play button to hear this message in audio format The probe into the spine-chilling triple murder case in Bengaluru in June has seen a fresh revelation. It has been found that one of the accused, Kenneth, took the help of a unique confidant to execute the murders — those of the parents and the sister of his live-in partner and the other accused Shwetha — an AI chatbot, constituting perhaps the first of its kind case in the country. Both the accused are techies. The city police have contacted the AI tool’s parent firm to know details of the chat history after their investigation unearthed that artificial intelligence was being used to make the sinister plan over almost six months, official sources said on Tuesday (July 21). ## Taking help of Google Gemini *India Today* cited the police telling it that Kenneth relied on Google Gemini to prepare his dangerous plan. It was also revealed that he had planned initially to use an iron furnace to get rid of the bodies. But on consulting the chatbot and weighing in other logistical issues, he allegedly decided against it. Police also said that Kenneth allegedly avoided asking the chatbot explicitly about how to commit a murder or how to dispose of a body. Instead, he chose to present hypothetical scenarios, framing his queries like if something had happened on those lines, what options did he have. Bengaluru Police reportedly wrote to Google requesting access to the history of Kenneth’s engagement with the AI tool. ## Killings took place on June 22 at Shwetha-Kenneth's house The ghastly killings took place at a rented apartment in Seegahalli in eastern Bengaluru, where 52-year-old Somasundar, his 48-year-old wife Muthulaxmi and their teenage younger daughter Supriya were stabbed to death. Shwetha, 24, is the couple's elder daughter. She fled the scene with Kenneth after the crime, and the duo was arrested separately from Puducherry, a few days later. Initial probe revealed that the alleged motive that led to the murders seemed to be financial disputes and strained relations between Shwetha and her family members. During interrogation, she accused her family of controlling her life, police said. The dispute worsened after Swetha allegedly failed to pay off a bank loan and notices started knocking on her parents’ doors. Somasundar and Muthulaxmi were also not happy with her relations with Kenneth. It was when her parents and sister went to the live-in couple’s residence to confront them that the attacks took place. The police said that after luring Muthulaxmi to their apartment on the fateful day, Kenneth stabbed her multiple times. Subsequently, when her husband and younger daughter arrived, they too were attacked fatally. Somasundar managed to reach the staircase despite his grievous injuries. He was noticed by neighbours, who alerted the police. In his dying declaration, he told police that he had been stabbed by his daughter and her live-in partner and urged them to rescue his wife and younger daughter before he was taken to hospital, where he later died. ## Kenneth confesses to using AI Kenneth told the police during interrogation that it was a trivial matter that led him to eliminate Shwetha’s family members. He conceded that he banked on the AI chatbot to guide him through a six-month plan to carry out the mission, the police said. The police subsequently wrote to Google to corroborate his version. Meanwhile, psychological assessments conducted during the probe revealed that Kenneth suffered from severe social isolation. Police alleged that Shwetha financially supported Kenneth while he remained socially isolated from friends and family. Police said Shwetha had earlier worked in the IT sector but lost her job after allegedly becoming increasingly influenced by Kenneth. After the murders, the accused duo allegedly went to Shwetha's house, from where they stole cash and silver ornaments before fleeing to Puducherry, they said. *(With agency inputs)* Next Story ## Similar Posts ## Top Stories

implementation.title: From Bengaluru to Florida: The troubling cases testing AI's ability to prevent violence
implementation.content: # From Bengaluru to Florida: The troubling cases testing AI's ability to prevent violence FP Tech Desk *•* July 22, 2026, 18:40:24 IST ## A string of high-profile criminal investigations has reignited questions over whether AI chatbots can detect and intervene when users exhibit signs of planning violent crimes Advertisement Subscribe Join Us + Follow us On Google hacker While ChatGPT, Grok and Gemini are acclaimed for their ability to answer almost any question, do they possess a similar capability to identify problematic behaviour early on and prevent users from seeking assistance for acts of violence? As more users turn to AI to plan mass shootings, murders and other violent crimes, the question has taken on renewed significance. The latest example comes from Bengaluru, where AI has allegedly played a role in a gruesome triple murder case. STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD Police claim that 25-year-old Kenneth spent nearly six months consulting Google’s Gemini before allegedly murdering his live-in partner’s parents and younger sister. Investigators allege that he used the chatbot to gather information on methods of killing, removing bloodstains and disposing of bodies. According to the police, Kenneth allegedly bypassed Gemini’s built-in safety guardrails by avoiding direct questions. Instead, he framed his prompts as hypothetical scenarios, asking what a person would do in such situations rather than explicitly seeking instructions. The alleged conversations with Gemini have since become part of the investigation, with police seeking access to his chat history with the AI assistant. However, the allegations are yet to be examined or tested in court. This is not the first time AI has allegedly featured in the planning of a violent crime. Several similar cases have surfaced in the United States and other countries. ### 2025 Florida State University mass shooting (United States) One of the most closely watched cases involving AI is the 2025 Florida State University mass shooting. According to a lawsuit filed by the family of one of the victims, the alleged gunman exchanged hundreds of conversations with ChatGPT in the months leading up to the attack. The suit claims the chatbot provided information related to planning the shooting, and prosecutors later reviewed the chat logs as part of the investigation. Florida Attorney James Uthmeier also launched a criminal investigation into ChatGPT’s alleged role. STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD In a case from Australia, court documents allege that a 13-year-old repeatedly used generative AI tools to create detailed mass shooting scenarios, draft violent manifestos and request a fictional story describing a “Bondi-style” beach massacre. Investigators said the alleged target was a school, but police arrested the teenager before any attack could be carried out. The AI-generated conversations later became part of the investigation. ### 2025 Cybertruck explosion (United States) Another high-profile case emerged after the 2025 Cybertruck explosion outside the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas. Investigators alleged that former U.S. Army soldier Matthew Livelsberger used ChatGPT to research explosives, tactical information and other details before carrying out the attack. Authorities later cited the chatbot interactions as part of the investigation. **Sam Altman’s Apology** OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has also publicly apologized over the company’s handling of one such case. In a letter to officials in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, Altman expressed regret that OpenAI failed to alert law enforcement after banning the ChatGPT account of 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar months before the February 2025 school shooting. The attack left the suspect’s mother, stepbrother, five students and an educator dead before the shooter died by suicide. Altman acknowledged the irreversible loss suffered by the community and said OpenAI should have done more after identifying the account as violating its policies. implementation.title: "Roadmap to murder:" engineer spent 6 months asking AI how to kill
implementation.content: # "Roadmap to murder:" engineer spent 6 months asking AI how to kill Contains sensitive details. Crime Scene. Hindustan Times via Getty Images. Marcus Walsh Journalist July 20, 2026 Updated: July 21, 2026 Key takeaways: * Police allege the suspect used an AI chatbot to research killing methods, body disposal and cleaning bloodstains. * Investigators have requested six months of chatbot logs to support the prosecution's digital evidence. * Police say financial strain and family resentment drove the alleged triple murder plot. * Detectives believe extreme social isolation helped the pair lose sight of real-world consequences. Key Takeaways by nexos.ai, reviewed by Cybernews staff. **An engineer and his partner reportedly committed a triple murder in Bengaluru, India, spending 6 months consulting a popular AI chatbot before the killings.** Police allege the engineer sought advice on how to murder, as well as methods for getting rid of bodies and removing bloodstains. Investigators say that nearly every stage of the alleged plot was researched through AI conversations, with police claiming the suspect, Kenneth, even asked about burning bodies after building an iron furnace intended for a planned cloud kitchen, a commercial kitchen used to prepare food for delivery only. Kenneth and his partner, Shwetha Somasundar, both aged 25, were arrested by local police after the June 22nd murders of Shwetha's mother, father, and younger sister. Police say the chatbot was a "roadmap" that helped shape the alleged plan, and have requested the suspect's complete AI chat history from the platform's parent company, which so far remains unnamed. As reported in *The Indian Express*, the police statement described: > “When the murder thought entered his head, he consulted the AI tool, which indicated the merits and demerits of incinerating bodies before disposal.” ## Financial and resentful motives The alleged motive centered on money, family conflict, and resentment toward his partner Shwetha's mother, with claims that Shwetha feared having to repay roughly 5 million Indian rupees (around $60,000) borrowed from her mother. The mother, Muthulakshmi, was lured to the apartment first before allegedly being stabbed 26 times. Subsequently, Shwetha's father and younger sister allegedly arrived separately and were also attacked. Police say the suspects later traveled to Shwetha's parental home in southeast Bengaluru to steal cash and silver ornaments before fleeing to nearby Puducherry. Here, they also discarded the younger sister Supriya's mobile phone. # Has your password leaked? Enter your password to check if it has leaked. Having a leaked password creates the risk of identity theft, financial damages, and worse! Crucially, the case turned when father Somasundar crawled from the apartment, blood-soaked, as neighbors found him lying on the staircase. He identified both suspects before dying in the hospital. Police describe both suspects as living in extreme social isolation despite professional backgrounds, claiming Kenneth had become largely cut off from friends while Shwetha became financially dependent on him. Shwetha had previously held a job at an international social media news company, but became more isolated after losing it. And according to police, the pair processed real-world consequences as if they were playing a computer game, with AI seemingly playing a major role in it. He has more than a decade of experience as a writer and editor and writes The Cosmic Report, Cybernews’ weekly space column.

Switch To Beeps Mode The prime accused in the Bengaluru triple murder case allegedly used Google's AI chatbot Gemini to research weapons, body disposal, poisoning and ways to evade police detection while planning the crime, according to Whitefield Division Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP) Saidulu Adavath. Speaking to NDTV, DCP Adavath said investigators found that the accused had used Google Gemini to create hypothetical scenarios and seek information related to committing crimes. The scenarios included "What if people come to my house?", "How do I attack them?" “He was using Google Gemini. He created hypothetical situations and searched for information about weapons, how to burn a body, how to stay without using a mobile phone and similar topics. He even sought details on different types of weapons and how slow poisoning works,” he said. Police also alleged that the accused had planned to destroy evidence by setting up a furnace. “He wanted to start a cloud kitchen. He had procured equipment, including a furnace and a tank, and had set them up. The plan was to use them to dispose of the body,” the DCP said. By then, the father and sister came to the door. He stabbed the father. When the sister raised an alarm, he turned towards her and stabbed her as well. She collapsed, while the father managed to run downstairs despite sustaining stab injuries,” he said. Advertisement Speaking about the role of the accused's partner, the officer said she was allegedly aware of the conspiracy. “She was present and was aware of what was happening. She knew about the planning,” he said. On the alleged motive, Adavath said the accused told investigators that financial problems and pressure from the woman's family had contributed to the crime. “The accused told us he had used the girl's money. She also did not want to return to her family and disliked them. They were under pressure from her family and, according to the accused, that was one of the reasons behind the crime,” he said. Police are now following the legal process to obtain the accused's search history from Google. “We believe a request has already been sent to Google. It requires a legal process, and the necessary application has to be made through proper legal channels,” the DCP said. The accused's electronic devices have also been seized and sent for forensic examination. “We do not have screenshots of the chats. The devices have been seized and sent for forensic examination,” Adavath said. It's regulators applying existing laws to AI. This month alone, the FTC proposed guidance suggesting undisclosed manipulation of AI outputs could raise deception concerns and continues to pursue AI-related enforcement using authorities that pre-date ChatGPT by decades. While organizations wait for comprehensive AI regulation, agencies appear increasingly comfortable using the tools they already have: • Consumer protection laws • Privacy laws • Unfair and deceptive practices standards • Existing cybersecurity obligations In other words, the legal question is no longer whether AI will be regulated. The question is whether your organization recognizes it's already being regulated. To view or add a comment, sign in * AI is rapidly changing how law enforcement prevents and responds to crime. Not anymore. As AI-generated images, videos, voices and documents become increasingly realistic, we are entering an era where AI won’t only create new legal risks, it may become the perfect excuse for human misconduct. Imagine someone assaulting people, stealing, publishing defamatory content, defrauding people online, then saying: “It wasn’t me, someone definitely used AI to generate it.” The danger isn’t simply whether AI can produce convincing content. It’s whether bad actors will weaponize AI to escape accountability. This raises difficult legal and human rights questions. Who bears the burden of proof? How do courts distinguish genuine AI-generated material from deliberate deception? How do we protect victims without undermining the presumption of innocence? Can digital forensics keep pace with generative AI? Responsible AI isn’t only about regulating algorithms. It’s also about preventing humans from using AI as a shield against responsibility. We would not normally blame a knife manufacturer when someone uses a knife to commit a crime. But what if the buyer walks into the shop, explains exactly whom he intends to harm, and the seller hands him the weapon anyway? That is where the analogy with AI becomes uncomfortable. AI searches reveal Bengaluru triple murder plot ## Police allege the murders were meticulously planned, with the main accused, Kenneth, using Gemini to seek indirect advice on attacking and killing. Investigators claim he explored using an iron furnace to dispose of the bodies before abandoning the idea, and believed the killings would free him from financial pressure. advertisement New details emerge in Bengaluru triple murder case Sagay Raj Bengaluru,UPDATED: Jul 21, 2026 20:08 IST Barely a month after the Bengaluru triple murder case sent shockwaves across the city, police have revealed that the prime accused, Kenneth, had used Artificial Intelligence (AI) to research how to commit a murder and dispose of a body. In June, a 55-year-old man, his 48-year-old wife, and their 20-year-old daughter were stabbed to death at an apartment in Bengaluru's KR Puram area. advertisement During the preliminary investigation, police suspicion fell on the slain couple's 25-year-old daughter, Shwetha, and her live-in partner, Kenneth, who had both gone absconding. They were tracked down in Puducherry, where Shwetha was taken into custody on June 24, followed by Kenneth's arrest a day later, on June 25. Now, a month later, police sources have disclosed that Kenneth had used Google's AI assistant, Gemini, to research how to commit a murder. According to police, Kenneth did not ask direct questions such as, "How do I dispose of a body?" or "How do I commit a murder?" Instead, he allegedly framed his queries indirectly, asking questions along the lines of, "If something like this happens, what should I do?" Police further said Kenneth used only Gemini for his searches. According to investigators, he had initially planned to use an iron furnace that he had purchased for a proposed cloud kitchen venture to dispose of the bodies. However, he later realised that the idea was not practically feasible. advertisement Police also said Kenneth allegedly asked Gemini questions such as, "Thieves came into my house. How do I attack them? What are the weapons?" According to police sources, he also searched for ways to first blind a person and then stab them, attempting to obtain information through the AI chatbot. Police said the iron furnace had originally been purchased for the proposed cloud kitchen. Later, according to police, Kenneth considered using it to dispose of the bodies and made certain arrangements with that objective in mind. challenges.title: Bengaluru accused used Google Gemini to plan 3 murders, he is not alone in seeking deadly advice from AI
challenges.content: # Bengaluru accused used Google Gemini to plan 3 murders, he is not alone in seeking deadly advice from AI ## Kenneth Arun Kumar reportedly used Google Gemini to plan murder of three people. As AI enters our lives, increasingly people are asking ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude for deadly advice and in some cases are even receiving "helpful" tips from the AI tools. Advertisement Bengaluru Police allege the triple murder accused spent six months using Google Gemini to plan the killings. Divya Bhati New Delhi,UPDATED: Jul 22, 2026 13:44 IST AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Grok can answer almost anything. Need recipe ideas? Ask AI. Need help writing code? Ask AI. But as it turns out, some people are turning to AI for something far more sinister. From mass shootings to cold-blooded murders, AI is increasingly showing up as a tool that many people are using while planning violent crimes. And in some cases, they are even getting the answers back with AI tools trying to be “helpful” in whatever their users are trying to do. advertisement ❮❯ The latest example comes from Bengaluru, where cops claim that 25-year-old Kenneth spent nearly six months consulting Google's Gemini before allegedly murdering his live-in partner's parents and younger sister. Investigators claim he used the chatbot to gather information on killing methods, removing bloodstains, disposing of bodies and even whether an iron furnace could be used to destroy evidence. But don't AI chatbots have guardrails? They do. So how does someone get around them? Well, they are tricking the AI bot. Police believe Kenneth allegedly avoided asking direct questions such as, "How do I commit murder?" Instead, he framed his prompts as hypothetical scenarios, asking what someone should do "if something like this happens". Investigators say that helped him gather information without triggering obvious safety filters. Cops also allege that he initially considered disposing of the bodies in an iron furnace built for his proposed cloud kitchen business before abandoning the idea after evaluating its practicality with Gemini. Police have now reportedly sought access to his Gemini chat history as part of the investigation. India Today Tech has reached out to Google for a comment and we will update the copy if and when we receive inputs. Note that the allegations are yet to be tested in court. However, the Bengaluru case is far from an isolated incident. From the US to Australia, investigators have uncovered several cases in which suspects allegedly turned to AI chatbots to research attacks, refine violent plans or obtain tactical information before committing crimes. ### 2025 Florida State University mass shooting One of the recent international cases that came into light due to AI connection is the 2025 Florida State University mass shooting. According to a lawsuit filed by the family of one of the victims, the alleged shooter exchanged hundreds of conversations with ChatGPT in the months leading up to the attack. The lawsuit claims the chatbot provided planning-related information, while prosecutors later reviewed the chat logs as part of the investigation. Florida's Attorney also launched a criminal investigation into ChatGPT's role. OpenAI, however, rejected the allegations, saying ChatGPT only returned publicly available factual information and did not encourage or promote violence. ### Teen allegedly used AI to plan mass shooting in Australia advertisement The US isn’t the only place where AI allegedly has became part of a criminal investigation in a case. In Australia, court documents claim a 13-year-old repeatedly used generative AI to create detailed mass shooting scenarios, draft violent manifestos and even requested a story describing a "Bondi-style" beach massacre. The alleged target was a school, but police arrested the teenager before any attack could take place. The case also became one of the earliest examples of AI-generated conversations being used as evidence in an alleged terrorism-style investigation. ### 2025 Cybertruck explosion in the US Another case that caught global attention due to AI connection was the 2025 Cybertruck explosion outside the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas. According to a report by The Guardian, investigators revealed former US Army soldier Matthew Livelsberger used ChatGPT to research explosives and tactical information before carrying out the attack. ### Teen stabs 3 girls in Finland In another case, this time from Finland, a 16-year-old allegedly spent months planning an attack on his school, using a chatbot to help draft a manifesto and prepare for the assault. He later stabbed three teenage girls at a school in Pirkkala. Police said they examined the alleged AI-assisted manifesto as part of their investigation, with the suspect reportedly claiming he had planned the attack for around six months. advertisement ### The danger of easy access to AI Of course, AI is making everyday life easier for millions of people. It helps students study, developers write code, businesses automate routine work and professionals get more done in less time. But like any powerful technology, it is only as good as the intent of the person using it. With AI now just a few clicks away for almost anyone with an internet connection, the ease of access is becoming a growing concern for technology companies and law enforcement agencies alike. To mitigate the risks, AI companies have introduced stricter guardrails designed to stop chatbots from providing harmful information. But as the Bengaluru case and several others suggest, those guardrails aren't foolproof. Some users are finding ways around them by disguising dangerous requests as hypothetical scenarios. And many times, as smart as AI is, it is getting fooled by the intents of its human users. - Ends Published By: Divya Bhati Published On: Jul 22, 2026 13:44 IST

challenges.title: Bengaluru Triple Murder Case: How Kenneth Arun Kumar Allegedly Used AI To Plan The Crime
challenges.content: # Bengaluru Triple Murder Case: How Kenneth Arun Kumar Allegedly Used AI To Plan The Crime Bengaluru triple murder accused Kenneth Arun Kumar allegedly used an AI chatbot while preparing for the alleged killings, according to police. Here's what investigators claim they found. Vageesha Shrivastava Published on 21 / 07 / 2026 See also on Brut Artificial intelligence tools are now part of everyday life, helping people with research, work and learning. But a Bengaluru triple murder investigation has raised questions about the possible misuse of technology. Police alleged that software professional Kenneth Arun Kumar used an AI chatbot while preparing for the alleged murder of three members of his live-in partner’s family. Investigators claimed that the alleged plan developed over several months and involved digital tools. The case came to light after three members of Shwetha’s family were found dead at Kenneth’s apartment in Bengaluru’s Seegehalli area, under the K R Puram police station limits. Police later arrested Kenneth in Puducherry in connection with the case. ## **What Happened In The Bengaluru Triple Murder Case?** According to the police investigation, the victims were members of Kenneth’s live-in partner Shwetha’s family. Police alleged that Kenneth was involved in the deaths of Shwetha’s mother Muthulakshmi, her father and her brother following a personal dispute. Investigators claimed that the killings were planned and not an immediate act. During the probe, police examined Kenneth’s electronic devices, online activity and alleged conversations with an AI chatbot. The investigation focused on understanding the sequence of events and whether technology played a role in the alleged preparation. ## **A Six-Month Plan: How Police Say The Crime Was Prepared** Police sources claimed that the idea of targeting his partner’s family developed over time. Investigators alleged that Kenneth spent around six months preparing for the alleged crime and researching different aspects of the plan. Police claimed that he used an AI chatbot to ask questions related to the alleged crime. Investigators examined these digital interactions as part of the evidence collected during the probe. However, police have not claimed that AI acted independently. The allegation is that Kenneth used an available technology tool during the preparation process. ## **Why Did Kenneth Allegedly Plan The Killings?** Police are investigating relationship tensions, family disagreements and financial issues as possible reasons behind the alleged killings. According to The Indian Express, tensions had developed between Kenneth and Shwetha’s family over their relationship. Investigators claimed that Shwetha had differences with her mother Muthulakshmi and allegedly felt that her mother was controlling. Police are also examining a financial dispute involving the couple. Police sources claimed that Shwetha had allegedly borrowed around ₹50 lakh from her mother and spent the money on Kenneth. Investigators are looking into whether concerns over repayment and family disagreements contributed to the conflict. Police sources claimed that these issues continued to build over time and that Kenneth spent months preparing for the alleged crime. ## **The Cloud Kitchen Plan And Furnace Link** Police also examined details related to Kenneth’s cloud kitchen plan during the investigation. According to investigators, Kenneth had built an iron furnace as part of his plan to start a cloud kitchen. Police examined the furnace as part of the investigation and are looking into whether it had any connection to the alleged crime. Police said the furnace was originally built for Kenneth's proposed cloud kitchen. Investigators are examining whether it was later intended to be used in connection with the alleged crime. ## **Who Is Kenneth Arun Kumar?** Kenneth Arun Kumar was described by police as a software professional with a technical background. His knowledge of technology became a focus of the investigation after police alleged that he used digital tools while preparing for the alleged crime. Investigators examined his devices, online activity and AI interactions to understand his actions before and after the killings. ## **How Did Police Investigate The Case?** After the bodies were discovered, Bengaluru Police began collecting physical and digital evidence. Investigators examined Kenneth’s electronic devices, online records and other material to reconstruct the events leading up to the killings. Police also analysed alleged AI chatbot conversations as part of the digital evidence. Kenneth was arrested and booked in connection with the triple murder case. The evidence collected by investigators will be examined during the legal process. ## **What Does The Case Reveal About AI Misuse?** The Bengaluru triple murder case has raised questions about how artificial intelligence tools can be misused. AI systems are designed to assist users with tasks such as writing, learning and problem-solving. However, police said the investigation highlights how widely available digital tools can allegedly be misused by individuals accused of committing crimes. Investigators have not alleged that the AI system acted independently or encouraged the crime. Instead, they claim the accused used it while preparing for the alleged offences. The case does not suggest that AI planned or carried out the crime independently. Instead, it highlights a growing challenge around preventing the misuse of easily accessible technology while ensuring responsible use.

challenges.title: Bengaluru triple-murder co-accused used AI tool to plan killings, cops say, seek chat history
challenges.content: x Two techies allegedly killed three members of a family in Bengaluru on June 22, 2026, with the help of AI chatbot suggestions, investigations have revealed. Representative Photo: iStock # Bengaluru triple-murder co-accused used AI tool to plan killings, cops say, seek chat history ## In what could be India's first hi-tech murder, police say Kenneth quizzed the AI chatbot with hypothetical queries over 6 months; they now probe details The Federal 22 July 2026 3:49 PM IST Click the Play button to hear this message in audio format The probe into the spine-chilling triple murder case in Bengaluru in June has seen a fresh revelation. It has been found that one of the accused, Kenneth, took the help of a unique confidant to execute the murders — those of the parents and the sister of his live-in partner and the other accused Shwetha — an AI chatbot, constituting perhaps the first of its kind case in the country. Both the accused are techies. The city police have contacted the AI tool’s parent firm to know details of the chat history after their investigation unearthed that artificial intelligence was being used to make the sinister plan over almost six months, official sources said on Tuesday (July 21). ## Taking help of Google Gemini *India Today* cited the police telling it that Kenneth relied on Google Gemini to prepare his dangerous plan. It was also revealed that he had planned initially to use an iron furnace to get rid of the bodies. But on consulting the chatbot and weighing in other logistical issues, he allegedly decided against it. Police also said that Kenneth allegedly avoided asking the chatbot explicitly about how to commit a murder or how to dispose of a body. Instead, he chose to present hypothetical scenarios, framing his queries like if something had happened on those lines, what options did he have. Bengaluru Police reportedly wrote to Google requesting access to the history of Kenneth’s engagement with the AI tool. ## Killings took place on June 22 at Shwetha-Kenneth's house The ghastly killings took place at a rented apartment in Seegahalli in eastern Bengaluru, where 52-year-old Somasundar, his 48-year-old wife Muthulaxmi and their teenage younger daughter Supriya were stabbed to death. Shwetha, 24, is the couple's elder daughter. She fled the scene with Kenneth after the crime, and the duo was arrested separately from Puducherry, a few days later. Initial probe revealed that the alleged motive that led to the murders seemed to be financial disputes and strained relations between Shwetha and her family members. During interrogation, she accused her family of controlling her life, police said. The dispute worsened after Swetha allegedly failed to pay off a bank loan and notices started knocking on her parents’ doors. Somasundar and Muthulaxmi were also not happy with her relations with Kenneth. It was when her parents and sister went to the live-in couple’s residence to confront them that the attacks took place. The police said that after luring Muthulaxmi to their apartment on the fateful day, Kenneth stabbed her multiple times. Subsequently, when her husband and younger daughter arrived, they too were attacked fatally. Somasundar managed to reach the staircase despite his grievous injuries. He was noticed by neighbours, who alerted the police. In his dying declaration, he told police that he had been stabbed by his daughter and her live-in partner and urged them to rescue his wife and younger daughter before he was taken to hospital, where he later died. ## Kenneth confesses to using AI Kenneth told the police during interrogation that it was a trivial matter that led him to eliminate Shwetha’s family members. He conceded that he banked on the AI chatbot to guide him through a six-month plan to carry out the mission, the police said. The police subsequently wrote to Google to corroborate his version. Meanwhile, psychological assessments conducted during the probe revealed that Kenneth suffered from severe social isolation. Police alleged that Shwetha financially supported Kenneth while he remained socially isolated from friends and family. Police said Shwetha had earlier worked in the IT sector but lost her job after allegedly becoming increasingly influenced by Kenneth. After the murders, the accused duo allegedly went to Shwetha's house, from where they stole cash and silver ornaments before fleeing to Puducherry, they said. *(With agency inputs)* Next Story ## Similar Posts ## Top Stories
