Subsequently, when her husband and younger daughter arrived, they too were attacked fatally. Somasundar managed to reach the staircase despite his grievous injuries. He was noticed by neighbours, who alerted the police. In his dying declaration, he told police that he had been stabbed by his daughter and her live-in partner and urged them to rescue his wife and younger daughter before he was taken to hospital, where he later died. ## Kenneth confesses to using AI Kenneth told the police during interrogation that it was a trivial matter that led him to eliminate Shwetha’s family members. He conceded that he banked on the AI chatbot to guide him through a six-month plan to carry out the mission, the police said. The police subsequently wrote to Google to corroborate his version. Meanwhile, psychological assessments conducted during the probe revealed that Kenneth suffered from severe social isolation. Police alleged that Shwetha financially supported Kenneth while he remained socially isolated from friends and family. Police said Shwetha had earlier worked in the IT sector but lost her job after allegedly becoming increasingly influenced by Kenneth. After the murders, the accused duo allegedly went to Shwetha's house, from where they stole cash and silver ornaments before fleeing to Puducherry, they said. *(With agency inputs)* Next Story ## Similar Posts ## Top Stories

(48), father, Somasundar (54), and younger sister, Supriya (20). The three were allegedly killed at the couple's apartment in K R Puram on June 22. According to The Indian Express, Kenneth allegedly consulted the AI chatbot over nearly six months while planning the murders. Shwetha was remanded to judicial custody on July 10 after the completion of her police custody. Police said she has expressed willingness to make a confessional statement in exchange for a pardon. future.title: From Bengaluru to Florida: The troubling cases testing AI's ability to prevent violence
future.content: # From Bengaluru to Florida: The troubling cases testing AI's ability to prevent violence FP Tech Desk *•* July 22, 2026, 18:40:24 IST ## A string of high-profile criminal investigations has reignited questions over whether AI chatbots can detect and intervene when users exhibit signs of planning violent crimes Advertisement Subscribe Join Us + Follow us On Google hacker While ChatGPT, Grok and Gemini are acclaimed for their ability to answer almost any question, do they possess a similar capability to identify problematic behaviour early on and prevent users from seeking assistance for acts of violence? As more users turn to AI to plan mass shootings, murders and other violent crimes, the question has taken on renewed significance. The latest example comes from Bengaluru, where AI has allegedly played a role in a gruesome triple murder case. STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD Police claim that 25-year-old Kenneth spent nearly six months consulting Google’s Gemini before allegedly murdering his live-in partner’s parents and younger sister. Investigators allege that he used the chatbot to gather information on methods of killing, removing bloodstains and disposing of bodies. According to the police, Kenneth allegedly bypassed Gemini’s built-in safety guardrails by avoiding direct questions. Instead, he framed his prompts as hypothetical scenarios, asking what a person would do in such situations rather than explicitly seeking instructions. The alleged conversations with Gemini have since become part of the investigation, with police seeking access to his chat history with the AI assistant. However, the allegations are yet to be examined or tested in court. This is not the first time AI has allegedly featured in the planning of a violent crime. Several similar cases have surfaced in the United States and other countries. ### 2025 Florida State University mass shooting (United States) One of the most closely watched cases involving AI is the 2025 Florida State University mass shooting. According to a lawsuit filed by the family of one of the victims, the alleged gunman exchanged hundreds of conversations with ChatGPT in the months leading up to the attack. The suit claims the chatbot provided information related to planning the shooting, and prosecutors later reviewed the chat logs as part of the investigation. Florida Attorney James Uthmeier also launched a criminal investigation into ChatGPT’s alleged role. STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD In a case from Australia, court documents allege that a 13-year-old repeatedly used generative AI tools to create detailed mass shooting scenarios, draft violent manifestos and request a fictional story describing a “Bondi-style” beach massacre. Investigators said the alleged target was a school, but police arrested the teenager before any attack could be carried out. The AI-generated conversations later became part of the investigation. ### 2025 Cybertruck explosion (United States) Another high-profile case emerged after the 2025 Cybertruck explosion outside the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas. Investigators alleged that former U.S. Army soldier Matthew Livelsberger used ChatGPT to research explosives, tactical information and other details before carrying out the attack. Authorities later cited the chatbot interactions as part of the investigation. **Sam Altman’s Apology** OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has also publicly apologized over the company’s handling of one such case. In a letter to officials in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, Altman expressed regret that OpenAI failed to alert law enforcement after banning the ChatGPT account of 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar months before the February 2025 school shooting. The attack left the suspect’s mother, stepbrother, five students and an educator dead before the shooter died by suicide. Altman acknowledged the irreversible loss suffered by the community and said OpenAI should have done more after identifying the account as violating its policies. future.content: # AI chatbot comes under scrutiny in Bengaluru triple murder investigation ## Police allege a software professional used an AI chatbot over several months while planning the killings, prompting fresh debate over the limits of AI safety measures. By **Storyboard18**| July 24, 2026, 15:26:15 IST * Share ### Share this Article × WhatsAppFacebookTwitterLinkedinMail * Follow Us Bengaluru triple murder case puts AI chatbot guardrails under scrutiny The investigation into the alleged murder of three members of a Bengaluru family has raised new questions about how artificial intelligence tools can be misused and whether existing safety mechanisms are sufficient to prevent harmful use. According to investigators, 25-year-old software professional Kenneth Arun Kumar allegedly spent nearly six months interacting with an AI chatbot while planning the crime. Police claim he framed his questions as hypothetical situations to obtain information without triggering the platform's safety restrictions. Kenneth and his live-in partner, Shwetha, have been arrested in connection with the deaths of her parents and younger sister at their apartment in Bengaluru's KR Puram. Investigators believe the incident followed a dispute over an alleged unpaid loan of around ₹50 lakh. As part of the investigation, police are examining the accused's digital activity. Reports indicate that Kenneth allegedly sought information on topics including methods of incapacitating individuals, removing bloodstains using chemicals and disposing of bodies. Investigators are also reviewing searches related to whether an industrial furnace intended for a planned cloud kitchen could be used to destroy human remains. Officials told local media that the accused repeatedly interacted with the chatbot while refining the alleged plan. Police have reportedly contacted the company operating the AI platform to obtain conversation records that could form part of the digital evidence in the case. Investigators have not accused the AI platform of any wrongdoing. Instead, the focus has shifted to whether users can bypass built-in safeguards by rephrasing prompts or presenting harmful requests as fictional or academic scenarios. *(Inputs from CNBC TV18 report)* Follow Storyboard18 on Google for the latest and breaking digital news and industry updates, along with in-depth coverage of digital media and gaming news. By default, an AND relationship is assumed between Search Within terms unless you specify a different operator in the **Edit Query:** input. By default, an **OR** relationship is assumed between words within 1 Search Within term. #### Searching for phrases Enclose your search terms within **double** quotation marks (" ") to search for an exact match of that phrase. If no quotation marks are used, search results will be populated with publications that contain your search terms somewhere in the text. For example, if you search for *"machine learning"* the search engine will limit the results to publications that contain this exact phrase otherwise an **OR** will be assumed in between the words. Curly quotes (“ ”) are also acceptable eg. *“machine learning”* **NOTE 1:** opening and closing quotes must be of the same type; curly or straight. Please avoid entering *“machine learning"* **NOTE 2:** single quotation marks (' ') are ignored and will not return exact phrase matches. #### Wildcards Use an asterisk (\*) to specify any number of unknown characters. For example, if you search for **comput\***, the search engine will provide results that contain words such as compute, comput**ation**, comput**ing**, etc. Use a question mark (?) to specify any single unknown character. For example, if you search for **compute?**, the search engine will provide results that contain words such as computer or compute**d** but not compute**rs** because the question mark represents only one character. **NOTE**: Wildcards cannot be used at the start of a search term or when searching for phrases within quotes. #### Special Characters The following characters have a special meaning when they appear in a query: + - && || ! expert_views.content: Bengaluru Murder Probe Alleges AI Chatbot as Accomplice 🛰️ [SECURITY] Police allege AI chatbot aided Bengaluru triple murder. Why it matters: This case represents a critical juncture in understanding the potential misuse of AI, moving beyond theoretical discussions to real-world criminal application. It forces law enforcement and policymakers to confront how generative AI tools can be leveraged for malicious purposes, necessitating new strategies for digital forensics and content moderation. 🤔 What ethical responsibilities do AI developers have in preventing their models from being used for criminal planning? #AICrime #GenerativeAIMisuse #DigitalForensics #AIEthics #LawEnforcement 📡 Follow DailyAIWire for high-signal AI news. # Daily AI Wire News’ Post ## More Relevant Posts * The biggest AI regulatory development in 2026 isn't a new AI law. It's regulators applying existing laws to AI. This month alone, the FTC proposed guidance suggesting undisclosed manipulation of AI outputs could raise deception concerns and continues to pursue AI-related enforcement using authorities that pre-date ChatGPT by decades. While organizations wait for comprehensive AI regulation, agencies appear increasingly comfortable using the tools they already have: • Consumer protection laws • Privacy laws • Unfair and deceptive practices standards • Existing cybersecurity obligations In other words, the legal question is no longer whether AI will be regulated. The question is whether your organization recognizes it's already being regulated. To view or add a comment, sign in * AI is rapidly changing how law enforcement prevents and responds to crime. From machine learning tools that spot patterns in data to technologies that help detect fraud and deepen investigations, today’s AI offers powerful new capabilities—alongside real concerns around privacy, ethics, and misuse. However, there is a dangerous “governance deficit”—nearly half of the surveyed Fortune 1000 companies admit they do not have a formal risk governance framework to regulate AI use. Not anymore. As AI-generated images, videos, voices and documents become increasingly realistic, we are entering an era where AI won’t only create new legal risks, it may become the perfect excuse for human misconduct. Imagine someone assaulting people, stealing, publishing defamatory content, defrauding people online, then saying: “It wasn’t me, someone definitely used AI to generate it.” The danger isn’t simply whether AI can produce convincing content. It’s whether bad actors will weaponize AI to escape accountability. This raises difficult legal and human rights questions. Who bears the burden of proof? How do courts distinguish genuine AI-generated material from deliberate deception? How do we protect victims without undermining the presumption of innocence? Can digital forensics keep pace with generative AI? Responsible AI isn’t only about regulating algorithms. It’s also about preventing humans from using AI as a shield against responsibility. The question may soon change from “Can AI commit harm?” to “Can humans hide behind AI to avoid liability?” I suspect that will become one of the defining legal questions of this decade. As organizations increasingly rely on AI for decision-making, documentation, and investigations, understanding legal responsibility is more important than ever. It explores the importance of AI governance, ethical accountability, and human oversight in AI-driven decisions. Featuring insights by Lili Kazemi from 𝐀𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐭, with a law enforcement AI perspective from Christopher Ryan of policereports.ai, this article offers valuable perspectives on the evolving role of AI in legal accountability. 🔍 Key Highlights: ✅ AI-generated evidence and its legal implications. ✅ The importance of AI governance and compliance. ✅ Why human oversight is essential for responsible AI. 📖 Read the full article: https://lnkd.in/dtREN4-H #ArtificialIntelligence #AI #ResponsibleAI #AIGovernance #AICompliance #LegalTech #AIEthics #EnterpriseAI #Innovation To view or add a comment, sign in * An AI company should not be liable for everything a user does with its model. But it should not be allowed to hide behind that sentence either. xAI is now suing a man accused of deliberately bypassing Grok's safeguards to create sexualized deepfakes of real adults and children. I think suing him is justified. The person who intentionally creates and distributes illegal material should carry the primary responsibility. We would not normally blame a knife manufacturer when someone uses a knife to commit a crime. But what if the buyer walks into the shop, explains exactly whom he intends to harm, and the seller hands him the weapon anyway? That is where the analogy with AI becomes uncomfortable. An AI platform is not simply selling a passive object. It reads the request, generates the output and can recognize when someone repeatedly rephrases an obviously abusive prompt. It also controls the safeguards for every user, instantly and centrally. No company can prevent every attempt at misuse. Perfection is an impossible legal standard. But implementing meaningful guardrails against explicit requests for child sexual abuse material or non-consensual sexual imagery is not perfection. It is the bare minimum. From 2 August, the EU AI Act will require greater transparency around AI-generated content and deepfakes. That matters, but labelling tells us that something is synthetic. It does not settle who should have prevented the harm. So where should the legal line sit? If an AI refuses once but produces the same illegal content after a slightly different prompt, did the user bypass a safeguard, or did the company fail to build a meaningful one? #AIRegulation #Deepfakes #EUAIAct #AISafety #TrustAndSafety To view or add a comment, sign in * When AI 🤖 Becomes a Tool for Deception, Not Governance A sanitation officer in Gurugram allegedly used AI-generated images to show that an illegal garbage dump had been cleaned. The fake photographs were uploaded on the grievance portal as "proof of resolution" while the garbage remained untouched. The officer has now been terminated. This incident isn't just about one official. It's a warning. We are entering an era where seeing is no longer believing. AI was meant to help governments become smarter—predict garbage accumulation, optimize traffic, detect fraud, improve healthcare delivery, and make public services more efficient. Researchers have already demonstrated AI systems that can automatically detect and monitor waste dumping with over 90% accuracy. Instead, in this case, AI was allegedly used to: ❌ Fabricate evidence ❌ Mislead citizens ❌ Manipulate grievance redressal systems ❌ Create a false impression of governance And this is not an isolated concern. expert_views.content: # 'How to kill, remove bloodstains, dispose bodies': Bengaluru triple murder accused turned to AI chatbot BENGALURU: Investigators probing the sensational triple murder in Bengaluru have approached an artificial intelligence company for access to the accused’s chat history after discovering that he allegedly relied on an AI chatbot to plan the killings over nearly six months, police said on Tuesday. Police said Kenneth, 25, who has been arrested along with his live-in partner Shwetha, 24, allegedly used the chatbot at various stages of the crime, from seeking advice on how to kill and dispose of bodies to finding ways to erase evidence. The murders came to light on June 22, when Somasundar (52), his wife Muthulaxmi (48), and their younger daughter Supriya (19) were found stabbed to death in their apartment in Seegehalli under the KR Puram police station limits. Days later, Shwetha and Kenneth, who had allegedly fled Bengaluru after the murders, were arrested separately in Puducherry, where they had been hiding to evade police. Investigators suspect that financial disputes and strained family relations lay behind the killings. According to police, Shwetha allegedly borrowed Rs 50 lakh from her mother to help Kenneth set up a cloud kitchen business, but the money was exhausted, triggering fears over repayment. While police believe the couple acted together, Kenneth allegedly led the planning and execution of the murders. A senior police officer said he consulted the AI chatbot throughout the six-month period, asking questions about killing methods, body disposal, bloodstain removal and whether a furnace built for the proposed business could be used to incinerate the bodies. During questioning, Kenneth allegedly admitted that a minor disagreement had prompted him to target Shwetha’s family and confessed to depending heavily on the chatbot for guidance. Police have now written to the AI company seeking digital evidence of Kenneth’s conversations with the tool to corroborate his statements. The probe has also revealed that Kenneth suffered from severe social isolation, according to psychological assessments conducted during the investigation. Police alleged that Shwetha financially supported him and gradually distanced herself from friends and family, eventually losing her job in the IT sector. Investigators said the accused duo stole cash and silver ornaments from Shwetha’s house after the murders before escaping to Puducherry. Police said Kenneth allegedly lured Muthulaxmi to the apartment on June 22 and stabbed her repeatedly. Her husband and younger daughter were attacked when they arrived at the scene. Despite sustaining grievous injuries, Somasundar managed to reach the staircase, where neighbours spotted him and alerted police. In his dying declaration, he allegedly identified his daughter and her live-in partner as the attackers and urged police to save his wife and younger daughter before succumbing to his injuries in hospital. expert_views.title: Bengaluru accused used Google Gemini to plan 3 murders, he is not alone in seeking deadly advice from AI
expert_views.content: # Bengaluru accused used Google Gemini to plan 3 murders, he is not alone in seeking deadly advice from AI ## Kenneth Arun Kumar reportedly used Google Gemini to plan murder of three people. As AI enters our lives, increasingly people are asking ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude for deadly advice and in some cases are even receiving "helpful" tips from the AI tools. Advertisement Bengaluru Police allege the triple murder accused spent six months using Google Gemini to plan the killings. Divya Bhati New Delhi,UPDATED: Jul 22, 2026 13:44 IST AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Grok can answer almost anything. Need recipe ideas? Ask AI. Need help writing code? Ask AI. But as it turns out, some people are turning to AI for something far more sinister. From mass shootings to cold-blooded murders, AI is increasingly showing up as a tool that many people are using while planning violent crimes. And in some cases, they are even getting the answers back with AI tools trying to be “helpful” in whatever their users are trying to do. advertisement ❮❯ The latest example comes from Bengaluru, where cops claim that 25-year-old Kenneth spent nearly six months consulting Google's Gemini before allegedly murdering his live-in partner's parents and younger sister. Investigators claim he used the chatbot to gather information on killing methods, removing bloodstains, disposing of bodies and even whether an iron furnace could be used to destroy evidence. But don't AI chatbots have guardrails? They do. So how does someone get around them? Well, they are tricking the AI bot. Police believe Kenneth allegedly avoided asking direct questions such as, "How do I commit murder?" Instead, he framed his prompts as hypothetical scenarios, asking what someone should do "if something like this happens". Investigators say that helped him gather information without triggering obvious safety filters. Cops also allege that he initially considered disposing of the bodies in an iron furnace built for his proposed cloud kitchen business before abandoning the idea after evaluating its practicality with Gemini. Police have now reportedly sought access to his Gemini chat history as part of the investigation. India Today Tech has reached out to Google for a comment and we will update the copy if and when we receive inputs. Note that the allegations are yet to be tested in court. However, the Bengaluru case is far from an isolated incident. From the US to Australia, investigators have uncovered several cases in which suspects allegedly turned to AI chatbots to research attacks, refine violent plans or obtain tactical information before committing crimes. ### 2025 Florida State University mass shooting One of the recent international cases that came into light due to AI connection is the 2025 Florida State University mass shooting. According to a lawsuit filed by the family of one of the victims, the alleged shooter exchanged hundreds of conversations with ChatGPT in the months leading up to the attack. The lawsuit claims the chatbot provided planning-related information, while prosecutors later reviewed the chat logs as part of the investigation. Florida's Attorney also launched a criminal investigation into ChatGPT's role. OpenAI, however, rejected the allegations, saying ChatGPT only returned publicly available factual information and did not encourage or promote violence. ### Teen allegedly used AI to plan mass shooting in Australia advertisement The US isn’t the only place where AI allegedly has became part of a criminal investigation in a case. In Australia, court documents claim a 13-year-old repeatedly used generative AI to create detailed mass shooting scenarios, draft violent manifestos and even requested a story describing a "Bondi-style" beach massacre. The alleged target was a school, but police arrested the teenager before any attack could take place. The case also became one of the earliest examples of AI-generated conversations being used as evidence in an alleged terrorism-style investigation. ### 2025 Cybertruck explosion in the US Another case that caught global attention due to AI connection was the 2025 Cybertruck explosion outside the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas. According to a report by The Guardian, investigators revealed former US Army soldier Matthew Livelsberger used ChatGPT to research explosives and tactical information before carrying out the attack. ### Teen stabs 3 girls in Finland In another case, this time from Finland, a 16-year-old allegedly spent months planning an attack on his school, using a chatbot to help draft a manifesto and prepare for the assault. He later stabbed three teenage girls at a school in Pirkkala. Police said they examined the alleged AI-assisted manifesto as part of their investigation, with the suspect reportedly claiming he had planned the attack for around six months. advertisement ### The danger of easy access to AI Of course, AI is making everyday life easier for millions of people. It helps students study, developers write code, businesses automate routine work and professionals get more done in less time. But like any powerful technology, it is only as good as the intent of the person using it. With AI now just a few clicks away for almost anyone with an internet connection, the ease of access is becoming a growing concern for technology companies and law enforcement agencies alike. To mitigate the risks, AI companies have introduced stricter guardrails designed to stop chatbots from providing harmful information. But as the Bengaluru case and several others suggest, those guardrails aren't foolproof. Some users are finding ways around them by disguising dangerous requests as hypothetical scenarios. And many times, as smart as AI is, it is getting fooled by the intents of its human users. - Ends Published By: Divya Bhati Published On: Jul 22, 2026 13:44 IST

expert_views.title: Bengaluru Triple Murder Case: How Kenneth Arun Kumar Allegedly Used AI To Plan The Crime
expert_views.content: # Bengaluru Triple Murder Case: How Kenneth Arun Kumar Allegedly Used AI To Plan The Crime Bengaluru triple murder accused Kenneth Arun Kumar allegedly used an AI chatbot while preparing for the alleged killings, according to police. Here's what investigators claim they found. Vageesha Shrivastava Published on 21 / 07 / 2026 See also on Brut Artificial intelligence tools are now part of everyday life, helping people with research, work and learning. But a Bengaluru triple murder investigation has raised questions about the possible misuse of technology. Police alleged that software professional Kenneth Arun Kumar used an AI chatbot while preparing for the alleged murder of three members of his live-in partner’s family. Investigators claimed that the alleged plan developed over several months and involved digital tools. The case came to light after three members of Shwetha’s family were found dead at Kenneth’s apartment in Bengaluru’s Seegehalli area, under the K R Puram police station limits. Police later arrested Kenneth in Puducherry in connection with the case. ## **What Happened In The Bengaluru Triple Murder Case?** According to the police investigation, the victims were members of Kenneth’s live-in partner Shwetha’s family. Police alleged that Kenneth was involved in the deaths of Shwetha’s mother Muthulakshmi, her father and her brother following a personal dispute. Investigators claimed that the killings were planned and not an immediate act. During the probe, police examined Kenneth’s electronic devices, online activity and alleged conversations with an AI chatbot. The investigation focused on understanding the sequence of events and whether technology played a role in the alleged preparation. ## **A Six-Month Plan: How Police Say The Crime Was Prepared** Police sources claimed that the idea of targeting his partner’s family developed over time. Investigators alleged that Kenneth spent around six months preparing for the alleged crime and researching different aspects of the plan. Police claimed that he used an AI chatbot to ask questions related to the alleged crime. Investigators examined these digital interactions as part of the evidence collected during the probe. However, police have not claimed that AI acted independently. The allegation is that Kenneth used an available technology tool during the preparation process. ## **Why Did Kenneth Allegedly Plan The Killings?** Police are investigating relationship tensions, family disagreements and financial issues as possible reasons behind the alleged killings. According to The Indian Express, tensions had developed between Kenneth and Shwetha’s family over their relationship. Investigators claimed that Shwetha had differences with her mother Muthulakshmi and allegedly felt that her mother was controlling. Police are also examining a financial dispute involving the couple. Police sources claimed that Shwetha had allegedly borrowed around ₹50 lakh from her mother and spent the money on Kenneth. Investigators are looking into whether concerns over repayment and family disagreements contributed to the conflict. Police sources claimed that these issues continued to build over time and that Kenneth spent months preparing for the alleged crime. ## **The Cloud Kitchen Plan And Furnace Link** Police also examined details related to Kenneth’s cloud kitchen plan during the investigation. According to investigators, Kenneth had built an iron furnace as part of his plan to start a cloud kitchen. Police examined the furnace as part of the investigation and are looking into whether it had any connection to the alleged crime. Police said the furnace was originally built for Kenneth's proposed cloud kitchen. Investigators are examining whether it was later intended to be used in connection with the alleged crime. ## **Who Is Kenneth Arun Kumar?** Kenneth Arun Kumar was described by police as a software professional with a technical background. His knowledge of technology became a focus of the investigation after police alleged that he used digital tools while preparing for the alleged crime. Investigators examined his devices, online activity and AI interactions to understand his actions before and after the killings. ## **How Did Police Investigate The Case?** After the bodies were discovered, Bengaluru Police began collecting physical and digital evidence. Investigators examined Kenneth’s electronic devices, online records and other material to reconstruct the events leading up to the killings. Police also analysed alleged AI chatbot conversations as part of the digital evidence. Kenneth was arrested and booked in connection with the triple murder case. The evidence collected by investigators will be examined during the legal process. ## **What Does The Case Reveal About AI Misuse?** The Bengaluru triple murder case has raised questions about how artificial intelligence tools can be misused. AI systems are designed to assist users with tasks such as writing, learning and problem-solving. However, police said the investigation highlights how widely available digital tools can allegedly be misused by individuals accused of committing crimes. Investigators have not alleged that the AI system acted independently or encouraged the crime. Instead, they claim the accused used it while preparing for the alleged offences. The case does not suggest that AI planned or carried out the crime independently. Instead, it highlights a growing challenge around preventing the misuse of easily accessible technology while ensuring responsible use.

Days later, police arrested the couple’s elder daughter Shweta, 24, and her live-in partner Kenneth, 25, both engineers by profession, after tracking them to Puducherry, where they had gone into hiding. Investigators say that while both accused acted in tandem, Kenneth was responsible for the bulk of the planning and execution, and it is his alleged reliance on an AI chatbot, reportedly Google Gemini, that has drawn the case unusual attention. Police say he consulted the chatbot repeatedly over roughly six months, seeking guidance at various stages of the alleged conspiracy. ### How Investigators Say the Chatbot Was Used According to police, Kenneth avoided asking the chatbot direct questions about committing murder or disposing of a body. Instead, investigators allege he framed his queries as hypothetical scenarios, of the kind, “if something like this happens, what should someone do,” a pattern police believe was a deliberate attempt to extract relevant information without triggering the safety mechanisms most AI systems have built in for such requests. Police say the resulting conversations touched on planning the killings, destroying evidence, removing bloodstains, and evaluating whether an iron furnace Kenneth had built for a planned cloud kitchen business could be repurposed for body disposal. A senior officer told The Indian Express that investigators had “almost considered naming the AI chatbot as an accomplice,” given the extent to which Kenneth appeared to rely on it, though police have been clear that they are not attributing any legal liability to the AI tool itself. Bengaluru Police have formally written to Google seeking the underlying chat logs to corroborate Kenneth’s own account, given during interrogation, of how heavily he depended on the chatbot throughout the planning period. ### Financial Strain and Family Conflict at the Core The alleged motive traces back to money and mounting family tension. Police say Shweta had borrowed around ₹50 lakh from her mother to fund Kenneth’s cloud kitchen venture, a business that investigators believe failed to generate meaningful returns, leaving the loan largely unpaid even as pressure to repay it grew. Kenneth reportedly told police during interrogation that it was ultimately a “trivial” dispute that pushed him toward the killings, though the underlying pressure had clearly been building for months. Investigators say Shweta had separately expressed frustration with what she considered her mother’s controlling behaviour, a friction that had reportedly strained the family for some time, while psychological assessments during the probe found Kenneth had become severely socially isolated, relying almost entirely on Shweta for both emotional and financial support after leaving the IT sector. ### What the Case Signals for AI Oversight The episode has reopened debate around the safeguards built into mainstream AI platforms, which are generally designed to refuse or limit assistance connected to violent or illegal acts. Cybersecurity experts note that the case, if the allegations hold up, appears to illustrate how such safeguards can potentially be circumvented through indirect or hypothetical framing rather than explicit requests, a gap that developers of AI systems have been working to close as these tools see wider adoption. Renowned cybercrime expert and former IPS officer Prof Triveni Singh said the case underscores how emerging technologies can be misused when combined with clear criminal intent, even as the same tools deliver genuine value across productivity, research, healthcare and education. He said AI cannot replace human judgment or legal accountability, and noted that digital evidence, spanning chat records, cloud data, device forensics and online activity logs, is becoming an increasingly central pillar of modern criminal investigations, one police forces across India will likely need to build far greater technical capacity to handle. Police say the investigation remains ongoing as they await a formal response from Google and continue forensic verification of the digital evidence, with the precise role each accused played still being established before final charges are framed. #### Stay Connected

expert_views.content: # From Bengaluru to Florida: The troubling cases testing AI's ability to prevent violence FP Tech Desk *•* July 22, 2026, 18:40:24 IST ## A string of high-profile criminal investigations has reignited questions over whether AI chatbots can detect and intervene when users exhibit signs of planning violent crimes Advertisement Subscribe Join Us + Follow us On Google hacker While ChatGPT, Grok and Gemini are acclaimed for their ability to answer almost any question, do they possess a similar capability to identify problematic behaviour early on and prevent users from seeking assistance for acts of violence? As more users turn to AI to plan mass shootings, murders and other violent crimes, the question has taken on renewed significance. The latest example comes from Bengaluru, where AI has allegedly played a role in a gruesome triple murder case. STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD Police claim that 25-year-old Kenneth spent nearly six months consulting Google’s Gemini before allegedly murdering his live-in partner’s parents and younger sister. Investigators allege that he used the chatbot to gather information on methods of killing, removing bloodstains and disposing of bodies. According to the police, Kenneth allegedly bypassed Gemini’s built-in safety guardrails by avoiding direct questions. Instead, he framed his prompts as hypothetical scenarios, asking what a person would do in such situations rather than explicitly seeking instructions. The alleged conversations with Gemini have since become part of the investigation, with police seeking access to his chat history with the AI assistant. However, the allegations are yet to be examined or tested in court. This is not the first time AI has allegedly featured in the planning of a violent crime. Several similar cases have surfaced in the United States and other countries. ### 2025 Florida State University mass shooting (United States) One of the most closely watched cases involving AI is the 2025 Florida State University mass shooting. According to a lawsuit filed by the family of one of the victims, the alleged gunman exchanged hundreds of conversations with ChatGPT in the months leading up to the attack. The suit claims the chatbot provided information related to planning the shooting, and prosecutors later reviewed the chat logs as part of the investigation. Florida Attorney James Uthmeier also launched a criminal investigation into ChatGPT’s alleged role. STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD In a case from Australia, court documents allege that a 13-year-old repeatedly used generative AI tools to create detailed mass shooting scenarios, draft violent manifestos and request a fictional story describing a “Bondi-style” beach massacre. Investigators said the alleged target was a school, but police arrested the teenager before any attack could be carried out. The AI-generated conversations later became part of the investigation. ### 2025 Cybertruck explosion (United States) Another high-profile case emerged after the 2025 Cybertruck explosion outside the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas. Investigators alleged that former U.S. Army soldier Matthew Livelsberger used ChatGPT to research explosives, tactical information and other details before carrying out the attack. Authorities later cited the chatbot interactions as part of the investigation. **Sam Altman’s Apology** OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has also publicly apologized over the company’s handling of one such case. In a letter to officials in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, Altman expressed regret that OpenAI failed to alert law enforcement after banning the ChatGPT account of 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar months before the February 2025 school shooting. The attack left the suspect’s mother, stepbrother, five students and an educator dead before the shooter died by suicide. Altman acknowledged the irreversible loss suffered by the community and said OpenAI should have done more after identifying the account as violating its policies. expert_views.content: # "Roadmap to murder:" engineer spent 6 months asking AI how to kill Contains sensitive details. Crime Scene. Hindustan Times via Getty Images. Marcus Walsh Journalist July 20, 2026 Updated: July 21, 2026 Key takeaways: * Police allege the suspect used an AI chatbot to research killing methods, body disposal and cleaning bloodstains. * Investigators have requested six months of chatbot logs to support the prosecution's digital evidence. * Police say financial strain and family resentment drove the alleged triple murder plot. * Detectives believe extreme social isolation helped the pair lose sight of real-world consequences. Key Takeaways by nexos.ai, reviewed by Cybernews staff. **An engineer and his partner reportedly committed a triple murder in Bengaluru, India, spending 6 months consulting a popular AI chatbot before the killings.** Police allege the engineer sought advice on how to murder, as well as methods for getting rid of bodies and removing bloodstains. Investigators say that nearly every stage of the alleged plot was researched through AI conversations, with police claiming the suspect, Kenneth, even asked about burning bodies after building an iron furnace intended for a planned cloud kitchen, a commercial kitchen used to prepare food for delivery only. Kenneth and his partner, Shwetha Somasundar, both aged 25, were arrested by local police after the June 22nd murders of Shwetha's mother, father, and younger sister. Police say the chatbot was a "roadmap" that helped shape the alleged plan, and have requested the suspect's complete AI chat history from the platform's parent company, which so far remains unnamed. As reported in *The Indian Express*, the police statement described: > “When the murder thought entered his head, he consulted the AI tool, which indicated the merits and demerits of incinerating bodies before disposal.” ## Financial and resentful motives The alleged motive centered on money, family conflict, and resentment toward his partner Shwetha's mother, with claims that Shwetha feared having to repay roughly 5 million Indian rupees (around $60,000) borrowed from her mother. The mother, Muthulakshmi, was lured to the apartment first before allegedly being stabbed 26 times. Subsequently, Shwetha's father and younger sister allegedly arrived separately and were also attacked. Police say the suspects later traveled to Shwetha's parental home in southeast Bengaluru to steal cash and silver ornaments before fleeing to nearby Puducherry. Here, they also discarded the younger sister Supriya's mobile phone. # Has your password leaked? Enter your password to check if it has leaked. Crucially, the case turned when father Somasundar crawled from the apartment, blood-soaked, as neighbors found him lying on the staircase. He identified both suspects before dying in the hospital. Police describe both suspects as living in extreme social isolation despite professional backgrounds, claiming Kenneth had become largely cut off from friends while Shwetha became financially dependent on him. Shwetha had previously held a job at an international social media news company, but became more isolated after losing it. And according to police, the pair processed real-world consequences as if they were playing a computer game, with AI seemingly playing a major role in it.
